title: Learning How to Remember: Memory Modality Selection for GUI Agents

beats.text: Before you choose your foundation model, look at how Learning How to Remember beats the leader by 98.2%.
beats.visual_focus: Split screen showing an agent stalling on an OS desktop while an error flash highlights a single fixed memory buffer

beats.text: Static memory is the bottleneck: pure text logs blind models to spatial buttons, while stacking full-screen screenshots drowns context in visual bloat.
beats.visual_focus: Chalkboard comparison contrasting an ungrounded raw text stream against an overflowing stack of high-res screenshots choking token limits

beats.text: The eureka insight? Memory modality preference is strongly step-dependent. Enter SwitchMem, a dynamic routing framework that switches representations on the fly.
beats.visual_focus: Dynamic routing multiplexer node analyzing task state and toggling paths between visual tensor memories and tokenized text histories

beats.text: When clicking subtle UI icons, SwitchMem retrieves grounded visual memory. When parsing system commands or file paths, it switches to compact text tokens.

feynman_certification.listener_verdict: This was super clean and hooked me right away. Anyone who's tried building or playing with computer-use agents knows how fast they choke on UI clicks or burn context tokens on raw screenshots. Beat 4 made the mechanism click instantly: switching between spatial visual screenshots for clicking icons and raw text logs for things like file paths. No fluff, no robotic filler, just straight-up architecture insight.

thriller_metadata.physical_analogy: Driving across a city with either a blind written turn list or a cluttered satellite map instead of dynamically switching navigation views
thriller_metadata.paradigm_shift: Memory representation in GUI agents shifts from a static offline design choice to an active, real-time routing policy
